title: Improve Overall Safety
subtitle: Finding and removing hazards makes a home safer today. But a home does not hold still, and some harm cannot be prevented at all, only prepared for. This chapter completes the fourth S by adding what removing cannot: the moves that keep new dangers from taking hold, and the protections that stand ready for the day something goes wrong anyway. See it, remove it, prevent it, prepare for it, and the home is safe.

hands_off_note: Chapter 22 completes Safety, the fourth S. Chapter 20 opened the fourth S, taught the safety lens (could this hurt someone), and did a first pass on the obvious dangers. Chapter 21 made Safety thorough with the hazard hunt, a room-by-room walk carrying the five safety questions and removing each hazard on the spot. Chapter 22 delivers the two forward-looking moves a hazard hunt cannot make, and with them the fourth S is whole. It establishes that removing hazards alone is not enough, because a home does not hold still (the hunt is a snapshot, and new cords, new heights, and dead batteries flow quietly back) and because some harm cannot be removed in advance at all (a fire can still start, a person can still fall). So it raises the whole home's baseline rather than chasing hazards one at a time (the baseline reframe: not a longer list of dangers removed, but a home that is safer even against the ones you have not met yet). It teaches PREVENTION, keeping new hazards from taking hold by making the safe way the easy way, in three small habits (choose the safer default at the moment a thing arrives; give the dangerous things a home so away and safe are the same place; re-hunt lightly now and then to catch drift), carried by the prevention reframe and kept LIGHT, never a documented schedule. It teaches PREPARATION, readiness for the harm you cannot prevent (working smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms kept alive on every floor and near the bedrooms, a fire extinguisher within reach of the kitchen, a way out of every room and a walked exit plan to one meeting spot outside, and the few numbers and steps everyone knows), carried by the preparation reframe (the emotional core: preparation is love for the day you hope never comes). It brings the whole of Safety together as four moves, see, remove, prevent, prepare, with the goal of zero accidents and injuries read as a direction rather than a burden and safety consciousness as a steady, low, permanent household habit. Because completing Safety adds prevention and preparation rather than clearing everyday friction, the friction meter REACHES a marked SAFETY COMPLETE milestone, the fourth on the dial after Sort complete, Straighten complete, and Shine complete; the step onto the mark is small and honest, because the big daily friction was cleared long ago and what these three safety chapters removed was the friction of the worst day. worked_example.space: The whole home, now carrying the marks of readiness rather than the marks of dangers removed: a working smoke alarm, and a carbon-monoxide alarm where anything burns fuel, on every floor and near the bedrooms, kept alive; a fire extinguisher within reach of the kitchen; a safety shelf holding spare alarm batteries, a flashlight, and a first-aid kit in one known place; a walked exit plan from every bedroom to one meeting spot outside; and the few emergency numbers and steps everyone knows. Prevention keeps new hazards from taking hold: the heater bought is the one that switches itself off if it tips, the replaced cleaner runs out into a latched cupboard, the medicines live in one latched box, the knives live in the block, the button batteries live up high, and a slow walk with the five questions now and then catches the drift while it is small. The home is no longer defined by the dangers taken out of it; it is defined by what has been put into it, the protections that prevent new harm and stand ready for the harm no one can prevent.

the_two_moves_and_the_rule.raise_the_baseline: The hero. Removing hazards (Chapters 20 and 21) lowers the danger that is there; improving overall safety raises the whole home's floor, so it is safer even against the hazards you have not met yet. The baseline reframe, frozen: you can chase hazards one at a time forever, or you can raise the whole home's floor so it is harder to get hurt in at all; overall safety is the second thing, not a longer list of dangers removed, but a home that is safer even against the ones you have not met yet. Think of bailing a boat versus fixing the leak: removing hazards is bailing, necessary and endless because the water keeps coming; improving overall safety changes the boat itself so less water gets in and so you are ready if it does. Raising the baseline has two halves, prevention and preparation, and together they turn a home that has been made safe into a home that stays safe.
the_two_moves_and_the_rule.prevent: Keep new hazards from taking hold. A hunted home drifts back toward hazard not because anyone is careless but because ordinary life brings new things in, and some are dangerous, and they do not announce themselves. The prevention reframe, frozen: a hunt clears the hazards that are here, prevention is what keeps the next one from quietly taking their place, because a home does not stay hunted, it drifts, and things flow back in, and the only defense that scales is making the safe way the easy way. That last phrase is the whole of prevention, and it is the opposite of willpower: you will not keep a home safe by resolving to be more careful, any more than you kept it tidy by resolving to be neater; what works is design, steering the ordinary convenient decision toward safe. In practice, three small habits. Choose the safer default when something new comes into the house, at the one moment it is easiest, the moment it arrives (the heater that switches itself off if it tips, the cleaner that lives behind a latch). Give the dangerous things a home, the Straighten move aimed at safety, so away and safe are the same place and putting a thing away is what makes it safe (the medicines in one latched box, the knives in the block, the button batteries up high). And run the hunt again, lightly, now and then, a slow walk with the five questions, so drift is caught while it is small. The Prevent hero line, frozen: make the safe way the easy way, so hazards stop coming back: choose the safer default, give the dangerous things a home, and re-hunt now and then to catch what has drifted in. Nothing here is a schedule to be written down and enforced; that documented standard is a later S.
the_two_moves_and_the_rule.prepare: Ready for what you cannot prevent, the harder and gentler half, not about hazards at all. However well you prevent, some harm sits outside your reach: a fire in a wall you cannot see, carbon monoxide with no smell and no warning your body can catch, a fall on a night when nothing was wrong with the floor. You cannot remove these in advance, and pretending you can is not safety, it is just anxiety with extra steps; what you can do is prepare, so that on the day one of them comes the home meets it ready. The preparation reframe, frozen (the emotional core): some harm you cannot prevent, only prepare for; you cannot promise a fire will never start; you can promise that the alarm will wake you and that the way out is clear; preparation is love for the day you hope never comes. Preparation is a short and concrete list, not a state of dread. The center is the alarm, the one protection that has to work while you are unconscious: a working smoke alarm, and a carbon-monoxide alarm where anything burns fuel, on every floor and near the bedrooms, is the single highest-value thing in the chapter, and its whole value depends on being tested and its battery kept alive, or it is a plastic disc that does nothing. Beyond the alarm: a fire extinguisher within reach of the kitchen, where most home fires begin, and a rough sense of how to use it; a way out of every room, ideally two, and an exit plan the household has actually walked, from the bedrooms to a single meeting spot outside, so that in the dark and the noise nobody has to invent a plan; and the few plain numbers and steps everyone should know, including the children, so the knowledge does not live only in one head. The Prepare hero line, frozen: put the protections in place for the harm you cannot prevent: working smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms you keep alive, a fire extinguisher within reach, an exit everyone has walked, and the few numbers and steps everyone knows. Not a bunker. A prepared home.
the_two_moves_and_the_rule.the_rule: The rule, frozen: finding hazards makes a home safer once, preventing them and preparing for them keep it safe for good. Removing hazards makes a home safe now; prevention and preparation are what keep it safe. This is the definition of improving overall safety, frozen: the work beyond removing today's hazards, preventing new ones from taking hold and preparing for the harm you cannot prevent.

worked_example.applied_pass: Step back and look at the fourth S whole, because you have just finished it, and it turns out to have been four moves all along, each the answer to a question the one before it could not ask. You learned to see the hazard, by changing the question you asked the home from is it tidy to could this hurt someone. You learned to remove it, thoroughly, room by room, fixing each danger the moment you found it. You have now learned to prevent the next one, by making the safe way the easy way so the home stops drifting back. And you have learned to prepare for the harm that none of that can stop, so the home is ready on its worst day. See it, remove it, prevent it, prepare for it: not a checklist to run once, but a way of holding your home that, once you have it, you do not really put down. And notice what it is not: it is not the exhausting vigilance the last chapter warned against, the impossible job of watching everything forever. Each of the four moves is the opposite of vigilance, a piece of work you do deliberately, once or now and then, precisely so that you can stop watching. The professionals give the goal a stark name, zero accidents and injuries, and it can sound cold, but read it as a direction rather than a destination you will ever tick off; you will not achieve a mathematically perfect home, you are simply always turned that way, and being turned that way, with these four moves in hand, is what safety consciousness actually is: not fear held at a high pitch, but a steady, low, permanent habit of care that mostly runs quietly in the background of an ordinary, happy home.
